section_1.title: The Hook: An Unexpected Discovery
section_1.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive puzzle: How can a series of simple block collisions compute the digits of Pi? Present a visual of two blocks sliding on a frictionless surface towards a wall.
section_1.example: A small block (mass m) and a large block (mass M=100m) sliding on a frictionless floor.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
section_2.content: Briefly review Conservation of Momentum and Conservation of Kinetic Energy. Explain that elastic collisions between blocks follow these two laws, leading to a system of equations that define the velocity updates.
section_2.example: Visualizing a 'phase space' plot where the velocity of block A is the x-axis and block B is the y-axis, forming a circular arc path.

section_3.title: Geometric Mapping: The Circle Connection
section_3.content: Explain that the velocity states of the two blocks can be mapped onto a circle. As collisions occur, the velocity vector rotates by a specific angle. The total number of collisions corresponds to the arc length covered, mapping to Pi.
section_3.example: An animation showing the velocity vector rotating around a circle every time a collision occurs; the total rotation angle is proportional to the square root of the mass ratio.

section_4.title: Scaling Powers of 100
section_4.content: Demonstrate that as the mass ratio M/m increases by factors of 100 (100, 10,000, 1,000,000), the number of collisions matches the digits of Pi (3, 31, 314, etc.).
section_4.example: A digital counter display next to the colliding blocks showing the digits '3.14...' ticking up as the mass of the larger block increases.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Intuition
section_5.content: Synthesize why this works: The problem is a discrete manifestation of a continuous rotation in phase space. Conclude that Pi appears whenever we look at the 'geometry' of conservation laws.
section_5.example: A final visual summary: 1. Set up blocks, 2. Count collisions, 3. Reveal Pi.
